title: Washington Sanctions the Entire ICC Hours After a Former Court Judge Wins the Nobel Peace Prize, as the Houthis Kill 12 at Riyadh's Airport and Trump Weighs Joining the Yemen War
subhead: The US moves to defund and dismantle the International Criminal Court the same week it honors the court's former judge with a Nobel, splitting it from European allies — while a deadly Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia's main airport pulls Washington toward a wider Yemen campaign.

sections.heading: US Sanctions the Whole ICC — Hours After Its Former Judge Wins the Nobel
sections.body:
On Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sweeping US sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself, not just individual judges and prosecutors as in earlier rounds, per Al Jazeera and Reuters. Rubio said Washington would 'ban transactions with this rogue court', freeze any ICC assets held in US territory, and penalise companies that provide services to the court, which was established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. US firms were given a six-month grace period to wind down existing business.

The timing was pointed. The measures landed hours after South African jurist Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay, a former ICC judge now sitting on the International Court of Justice, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The Norwegian Nobel Committee said it chose her partly as a show of support for institutions under attack, warning that international law is 'under tremendous pressure' and that 'peace requires justice'. Rubio framed the campaign bluntly: 'Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC', pledging to keep dismantling it 'brick by brick'.

The trigger is the court's 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over suspected Gaza war crimes, plus an earlier US probe into Afghanistan. Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute, but the court can still prosecute their citizens for abuses committed on the territory of member states.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now openly trying to defund a Hague court that its own NATO allies fund and back. That converts a legal dispute into a live alliance fault line — European states, Canada, Japan and the UN have already rallied to the court — and signals that international accountability bodies can be targeted as instruments of hostile powers.

sections.heading: Houthis Kill 12 at Riyadh's Airport as Trump Weighs Joining the Campaign
sections.body:
A Houthi missile and drone attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, Saudi authorities said, according to the Associated Press, Reuters and Al Jazeera. Victims included four Saudis and eight foreigners; one American was among the dead, per the New York Post. Airport operations were suspended, and mass flight cancellations followed. It was the third strike on Saudi airport infrastructure this week.

Trump condemned the attack as 'terrible' and said the US is evaluating whether to join Saudi Arabia's retaliatory strikes on the Houthis. Al Jazeera reported that Trump also plans to call Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. A Saudi-led coalition said an air campaign against the Houthis is already under way in Yemen, and Ynetnews reported that Pakistan has joined the air campaign — extending, not closing, the Mecca Pact alignment that has been building for weeks.

The strike lands while Washington is still publicly weighing whether to restart direct strikes on Iran, the Houthis' principal backer, after the Riyadh escalation. Analysts quoted by the South China Morning Post warned the Saudi offensive risks pulling Riyadh into direct war with Tehran.
sections.whyItMatters: A mass-casualty strike on the Saudi capital's main airport forces Riyadh and Washington up the escalation ladder at the same moment the US is deciding whether to re-enter the Iran war. The Houthis are demonstrating they can still penetrate Saudi air defences and hit high-value civilian targets — a direct challenge to the Red Sea shipping corridor and Gulf energy infrastructure.

sections.heading: Trump Says Ukraine 'Should Get a New President' Amid the Diesel Deal Feud
sections.body:
Trump said Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war, suggesting Volodymyr Zelensky 'has not done enough' — comments made as tensions flared over a US-Russia diesel deal, per Al Jazeera, the BBC and the New York Times. Trump has tied the criticism to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, which he blames for high US diesel prices ahead of next month's midterms.

The deal, announced by Trump, would have Russia supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by a further 1.5 million tonnes, according to Al Jazeera. Zelensky told Axios the arrangement is 'not fair and not honest' and a 'gift to Putin'; Ukraine warned it would bankroll Russia's war. Russian strikes killed 20 in Ukraine the same day, and Ukraine hit a Russian fuel site hours after the deal was announced. GOP lawmakers have rejected the arrangement, per The Hill.

Separately, Putin told Trump that near-term peace talks remain unlikely, citing continued Ukrainian drone attacks — a message that undercut the 'productive' talks US officials described in Washington. The two-track diplomacy of last week has not produced movement on the battlefield.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump is now publicly calling for regime change in Kyiv while buying diesel from Moscow — an inversion that weakens Ukraine's leverage and hands Putin a sanctions-revenue lifeline at exactly the moment Washington is trying to broker an end to the war. It also exposes a deepening split with Congress and European allies over Russia policy.

sections.heading: Taiwan Plans an $850 Million Munitions Buyout as China Signals More Stimulus
sections.body:
Taiwan plans to spend roughly US$850 million to replenish ammunition stocks in preparation for a potential Chinese blockade, the South China Morning Post reported. Reuters described troops on the outlying islands key to Taiwan's defence preparing for a possible Chinese first strike, and the New York Times reported Taiwan is testing how it would resist a siege at sea. A RAND analysis noted China is exploring 'cognitive' warfare effects in its Taiwan planning, while an ACLED assessment said China's maritime presence around the island is becoming the new normal.

On the economic side, China signalled fresh fiscal support to counter a worsening slowdown, with Bloomberg describing it as a 'mini stimulus' likely sufficient to secure the GDP target but 'not much more'. Reuters reported Beijing pledged timely fiscal support and acknowledged 'prominent' imbalances; ING noted stronger growth and reflation have eased some pressure for a bigger package.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is running two clocks at once — a slow-burn military squeeze on Taiwan and a calibrated, minimal economic stimulus. Taiwan's munitions top-up shows Taipei reading the blockade risk as real and imminent rather than theoretical, while China's reluctance to spend big suggests it is preserving fiscal room for a longer confrontation.

sections.heading: Venezuela's Oil Becomes a US Instrument in the Americas
sections.body:
The Trump administration continues to fold Venezuela's oil sector into its hemispheric strategy after the US operation against Nicolás Maduro. Trump has publicly highlighted the Maduro capture alongside a subsequent oil deal with Venezuela, per NBC News, while PolitiFact flagged that he has offered an inflated figure for the US-Venezuelan oil gains. The Times reported a Venezuelan oilman under an overseas arrest warrant is now a key broker for the administration, and GIS Reports framed the 'Donroe' doctrine as a bid to push China out of the Americas.

The intervention has reshaped calculations across the region, with AS/COA compiling a wave of Latin American reactions and Politico arguing the Venezuela attack could change the wider geopolitical order. The dispute over Guyana's oil wealth, where Venezuela claims territory, remains live alongside the Venezuela file.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is converting a sanctions-and-arrest campaign into direct control over Venezuelan crude — extending the logic of US energy leverage from the Gulf to the Western Hemisphere. That pushes Beijing's access to Latin American oil onto the negotiating table and signals that the US will treat hemispheric energy as a strategic asset, not a market.

sections.heading: Gaza 'Ceasefire' Marks Its First Anniversary With Strikes Still Killing
sections.body:
A year to the day after the US-brokered Gaza ceasefire, Israeli attacks continued to kill Palestinians, Al Jazeera reported, including a child among eight killed on the anniversary. Hundreds of doctors demanded the World Medical Association suspend Israel, and mass pro-Palestinian marches were held in London, Rome and Berlin. Israel's economy has prospered through years of war even as prices worry voters, per Al Jazeera.

The anniversary is a reminder that the framework that once looked like a regional de-escalation has not stopped the fighting on the ground, even as the diplomatic arena shifts toward the ICC sanctions fight and the Yemen escalation.
sections.whyItMatters: A ceasefire that is nominally one year old but still produces daily casualties undermines the credibility of US-brokered frameworks at the very moment Washington is trying to extend its writ from Yemen to Iran. It also keeps the Gaza file — and the ICC warrants that triggered Friday's sanctions — as a permanent fault line in Western politics.

bottomLine: Today's defining move is Washington's decision to sanction the entire International Criminal Court, hours after a former ICC judge won the Nobel Peace Prize — an open attempt to dismantle a Hague institution that US allies fund, and the clearest sign yet that international justice is now treated as a battlefield. That plays out against a widening Middle East escalation: a Houthi strike killed 12 at Riyadh's airport, Trump is weighing joining the Yemen campaign, and the US is still deciding whether to re-enter the Iran war. On Ukraine, Trump's call for a 'new president' in Kyiv and his diesel purchase from Moscow have handed Putin leverage while splitting Washington from Congress and Europe. Looking ahead, the ICC sanctions will test whether Europe closes ranks to shield the court, and the Riyadh strike raises the odds that the US is drawn into a third simultaneous front.
